claim: Neurotransmitter:Sodium Symporters (NSSs) represent an important class of proteins mediating sodium-dependent uptake of neurotransmitters from the extracellular space.
source: The Neurotransmitter:Sodium Symporters (NSSs) represent an important class of proteins mediating sodium-dependent uptake of neurotransmitters from the extracellular space.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the function of NSS proteins.

claim: The substrate binding stoichiometry of the bacterial NSS protein, LeuT, and thus the principal transport mechanism, has been heavily debated.
source: The substrate binding stoichiometry of the bacterial NSS protein, LeuT, and thus the principal transport mechanism, has been heavily debated.
evidence: This statement references ongoing scientific debate, which is supported by the citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: High-quality NMR spectra of substrate bound to microcrystalline LeuT samples can be produced.
source: We were able to produce high-quality NMR spectra of substrate bound to microcrystalline LeuT samples and identify one set of sodium-dependent substrate-specific chemical shifts.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental NMR data showing spectra of bound substrate.

claim: One set of sodium-dependent substrate-specific chemical shifts was identified in LeuT.
source: We were able to produce high-quality NMR spectra of substrate bound to microcrystalline LeuT samples and identify one set of sodium-dependent substrate-specific chemical shifts.
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR spectroscopy data presented in the figures.

claim: The F253A mutant probes the major S1 binding site.
source: Furthermore, our data show that the binding site mutants F253A and L400S, which probe the major S1 binding site and the proposed S2 binding site, respectively, retain sodium-dependent substrate binding in the S1 site similar to the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is supported by prior literature and the experimental design of the study.

claim: The L400S mutant probes the proposed S2 binding site.
source: Furthermore, our data show that the binding site mutants F253A and L400S, which probe the major S1 binding site and the proposed S2 binding site, respectively, retain sodium-dependent substrate binding in the S1 site similar to the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is supported by prior literature and the experimental design of the study.

claim: The F253A and L400S mutants retain sodium-dependent substrate binding in the S1 site similar to the wild-type protein.
source: Furthermore, our data show that the binding site mutants F253A and L400S, which probe the major S1 binding site and the proposed S2 binding site, respectively, retain sodium-dependent substrate binding in the S1 site similar to the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Under the experimental conditions used, there is only one detectable leucine molecule bound to LeuT.
source: We conclude that under our experimental conditions there is only one detectable leucine molecule bound to LeuT.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the NMR data showing only one set of substrate signals.

claim: NSSs are responsible for clearing neurotransmitters such as dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, glycine and GABA from the synaptic cleft.
source: The Neurotransmitter:Sodium Symporters (NSSs) are responsible for clearing neurotransmitters, such as dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, glycine and GABA from the synaptic cleft.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about NSS function.

claim: NSSs are crucial for the regulation of synaptic transmission in the CNS.
source: The transporters are thereby crucial for the regulation of synaptic transmission in the CNS and alterations in their function have been linked to several psychiatric and neurological disorders such as depression, bipolar disorders, attention deficit hyperactive disorder (ADHD), epilepsy, and Parkinson's disease (Broer, 2013; Kristensen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Alterations in NSS function have been linked to several psychiatric and neurological disorders such as depression, bipolar disorders, attention deficit hyperactive disorder (ADHD), epilepsy, and Parkinson's disease.
source: The transporters are thereby crucial for the regulation of synaptic transmission in the CNS and alterations in their function have been linked to several psychiatric and neurological disorders such as depression, bipolar disorders, attention deficit hyperactive disorder (ADHD), epilepsy, and Parkinson's disease (Broer, 2013; Kristensen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references Broer, 2013 and Kristensen et al., 2011.

claim: The most detailed insight into structure-function relationships of NSSs comes from studies of the amino acid transporter, LeuT, from Aquifex aeolicus.
source: The most detailed insight into structure-function relationships of NSSs comes from studies of the amino acid transporter, LeuT, from Aquifex aeolicus (Kantcheva et al., 2013; Kazmier et al., 2014; Malinauskaite et al., 2014, 2016; Piscitelli et al., 2010; Quick et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2012a, 2012b; Yamashita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Recent structures of the drosophila dopamine transporter (dDAT) and the human serotonin transporter confirm that LeuT is a reliable model protein.
source: Recent structures of the drosophila dopamine transporter (dDAT) (Penmatsa et al., 2013) and the human serotonin transporter (Coleman et al., 2016), which are eukaryotic members of the NSS family, confirm that LeuT is a reliable model protein and proves its value in understanding the molecular function of this class of transporters.
evidence: This is supported by the cited structural studies.

claim: LeuT proves its value in understanding the molecular function of NSS transporters.
source: Recent structures of the drosophila dopamine transporter (dDAT) (Penmatsa et al., 2013) and the human serotonin transporter (Coleman et al., 2016), which are eukaryotic members of the NSS family, confirm that LeuT is a reliable model protein and proves its value in understanding the molecular function of this class of transporters.
evidence: This is supported by the cited structural studies and represents a consensus view.

claim: Functional studies of LeuT have suggested the existence of a secondary substrate binding site (S2) located in the extracellular vestibule of LeuT approximately 10 Å from the primary substrate binding site (S1).
source: Functional studies of LeuT have suggested the existence of a secondary substrate binding site (S2) located in the extracellular vestibule of LeuT approximately 10 Å from the primary substrate binding site (S1) (Khelashvili et al., 2013; Quick et al., 2009; Shi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited functional studies.

claim: The S2 site is suggested to be an allosteric trigger, essential for coupling the energy from the electrochemical gradient to the transport of the solute.
source: The S2 site is suggested to be an allosteric trigger, essential for coupling the energy from the electrochemical gradient to the transport of the solute.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior studies.

claim: The binding of leucine to the S2 site has been measured to have the same affinity (in nM range) as binding to the S1.
source: The binding of leucine to the S2 site has been measured to have the same affinity (in nM range) as binding to the S1 but does not, as the S1 bound substrate, directly coordinate sodium (Quick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference Quick et al., 2012.

claim: The S2 bound substrate does not directly coordinate sodium, unlike the S1 bound substrate.
source: The binding of leucine to the S2 site has been measured to have the same affinity (in nM range) as binding to the S1 but does not, as the S1 bound substrate, directly coordinate sodium (Quick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference Quick et al., 2012.

claim: Attempts to crystallize LeuT with substrate bound to the S2 site have so far been unsuccessful.
source: However, attempts to crystallize LeuT with substrate bound to the S2 site have so far been unsuccessful, and therefore the existence of the S2 site is supported primarily by radioligand binding assays and guided MD simulations (Quick et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of structural evidence, supported by the cited references.

claim: The existence of the S2 site is supported primarily by radioligand binding assays and guided MD simulations.
source: However, attempts to crystallize LeuT with substrate bound to the S2 site have so far been unsuccessful, and therefore the existence of the S2 site is supported primarily by radioligand binding assays and guided MD simulations (Quick et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Due to the lack of structural evidence, the existence of a high-affinity S2 site has been questioned.
source: Due to the lack of structural evidence, the existence of a high-affinity S2 site has been questioned (Piscitelli et al., 2010), supporting the need for employing new techniques for investigating ligand binding in NSS proteins.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference Piscitelli et al., 2010.

claim: Microcrystalline samples of LeuT were prepared under experimental conditions allowing for conformations capable of ligand binding to both S1 and S2.
source: We use microcrystalline samples of LeuT prepared under experimental conditions allowing for conformations capable of ligand binding to both S1 and S2 (Quick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on the cited reference and the experimental design.

claim: NMR offers information on the full structural ensemble which is unlikely not to include conformers (even lowly populated) prone to bind leucine in S2.
source: NMR offers information on the full structural ensemble which is unlikely not to include conformers (even lowly populated) prone to bind leucine in S2.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of NMR spectroscopy.

claim: Leucine binding to S1 and S2 may be distinguished by characteristic chemical shifts that are expected to be different due to different chemical environments.
source: Leucine binding to S1 and S2 may be distinguished by characteristic chemical shifts that are expected to be different due to different chemical environments, i.e. interacting residues (Reyes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on NMR principles and the cited reference.

claim: LeuT WT bound [3H]leucine with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 12 ± 1 nM in the presence of 200 mM sodium.
source: In scintillation proximity binding assays LeuT WT bound [3H]leucine with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 12 ± 1 nM in the presence of 200 mM sodium.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data from scintillation proximity binding assays.

claim: The EC50 value calculated for the Na+-dependent binding was 47 ± 4 mM.
source: The EC50 value calculated for the Na+-dependent binding was 47 ± 4 mM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The Kd and EC50 values are in agreement with those previously reported for LeuT.
source: These values are in agreement with those previously reported for LeuT (Shi et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited references.

claim: LeuT was purified and kept in the presence of 1 mM 15N enriched L-leucine to ensure substrate binding and detection in both sites.
source: As we were primarily interested in a simple readout reporting solely on substrate binding, we purified and kept LeuT in the presence of 1 mM 15N enriched L-leucine to ensure substrate binding and detection in both sites (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: With a 15N natural abundance around 0.3%, the background from the protein amides and amines is sufficiently low to distinguish even weakly populated states originating from the enriched substrate only.
source: With a 15N natural abundance around 0.3%, the background from the protein amides and amines is sufficiently low to distinguish even weakly populated states originating from the enriched substrate only.
evidence: This is based on known isotope abundance and NMR principles.

claim: One significant peak at 38.2 ppm was observed that could be assigned to the amine of protein bound leucine.
source: Using the microcrystalline preparations, we were able to produce the high quality CP-based 15N detected spectra showing one significant (above 2σ – Figure 1—figure supplement 4) peak at 38.2 ppm that could be assigned to the amine of protein bound leucine (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Broader signals between 110 and 130 ppm were observed, which originate from the 15N natural abundance of the LeuT amides.
source: In addition to the sharp signal from leucine, much broader signals between 110 and 130 ppm were also observed, which originate from the 15N natural abundance of the LeuT amides (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Sodium is required for leucine binding.
source: Sodium is required for leucine binding (Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: 23Na-NMR confirmed the presence of only a negligible amount of residual NaCl in the KCl sample.
source: By the use of 23Na-NMR we confirmed the presence of only a negligible amount of residual NaCl (at 7.1 ppm), and that no detectable Na+ was coordinated in the protein (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the 23Na-NMR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No detectable Na+ was coordinated in the protein in the KCl sample.
source: By the use of 23Na-NMR we confirmed the presence of only a negligible amount of residual NaCl (at 7.1 ppm), and that no detectable Na+ was coordinated in the protein (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the 23Na-NMR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the absence of Na+, the signal at 38.2 ppm in the 15N 1D spectrum disappeared.
source: In the absence of Na+, the signal at 38.2 ppm in the 15N 1D spectrum disappeared as expected for a signal originating from 15N-leucine bound to LeuT (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The amine NH3+ group of free leucine has a chemical shift of approximately 41 ppm at pH 8.
source: Worth of note, the amine NH3+ group of free leucine has a chemical shift of approximately 41 ppm at pH 8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–B), demonstrating that the bound substrate resides in a not fully solvent accessible environment.
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–B.

claim: The bound substrate resides in a not fully solvent accessible environment.
source: Worth of note, the amine NH3+ group of free leucine has a chemical shift of approximately 41 ppm at pH 8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–B), demonstrating that the bound substrate resides in a not fully solvent accessible environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the chemical shift difference between free and bound leucine.

claim: No signal from any additionally bound leucine was detected.
source: Importantly, we were unable to detect any signal from any additionally bound leucine.
evidence: This is based on the absence of additional peaks in the NMR spectra.

claim: The 13C CP/MAS spectra from the same samples clearly displayed only one single set of sodium dependent leucine signals.
source: Similarly, the 13C CP/MAS spectra from the same samples clearly displayed only one single set of sodium dependent leucine signals (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is directly supported by the 13C NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The final concentration of the added enriched substrate was lowered to 5 μM for the F253A and L400S mutant experiments.
source: For these experiments we lowered the final concentration of the added enriched substrate to 5 μM to ensure proper detimental effect by the mutations.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: A concentration of 5 μM has previously been reported not to provide any detectable [3H]leucine occupancy in the S2 site of LeuT L400S, but saturated S1 binding.
source: This concentration has previously been reported not to provide any detectable [3H]leucine occupancy in the S2 site of LeuT L400S, but saturated S1 binding (Quick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference Quick et al., 2012.

claim: For LeuT WT the specific leucine peak was unaffected by lowering the free leucine concentration.
source: For LeuT WT the specific leucine peak was unaffected by lowering the free leucine concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The F253A mutant has previously been shown to impair binding to the S1 site.
source: The F253A mutant has previously been shown to impair binding to the S1 site (Billesbølle et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: F253A serves as a S1 disturbing mutant at low substrate concentrations.
source: Thus, F253A serves as a S1 disturbing mutant at low substrate concentrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature and the experimental design.

claim: In the F253A 1D 15N spectrum, sodium dependent substrate binding was observed with a chemical shift of 38.4 ppm and a slightly lower signal intensity, when compared to the WT spectra.
source: In the F253A 1D 15N spectrum, we observed sodium dependent substrate binding with a chemical shift of 38.4 ppm and a slightly lower signal intensity, when compared to the WT spectra (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The shift in F253A was consistent for both high (1 mM) and low (5 µM) leucine concentrations.
source: The shift in F253A was consistent for both high (1 mM) and low (5 µM) leucine concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The chemical shift difference of ~0.2 ppm for the observed bound leucine peak demonstrates that the ligand is affected by the local environment of the S1 binding site.
source: Most importantly, the chemical shift difference of ~0.2 ppm for the observed bound leucine peak, demonstrates that the ligand is affected by the local environment of the S1 binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the chemical shift difference observed in the F253A mutant.

claim: The L400S mutation was previously suggested to abolish S2 leucine binding.
source: The L400S mutation was previously suggested to abolish S2 leucine binding (Quick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference Quick et al., 2012.

claim: The 15N spectrum obtained for leucine bound to L400S completely resembled the spectrum obtained with WT protein.
source: The 15N spectrum obtained for leucine bound to L400S (Figure 2C, blue) completely resembled the spectrum obtained with WT protein (Figure 2C, red).
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No change in intensity or chemical shift was detected for L400S compared to WT.
source: We were not able to detect any change in intensity or chemical shift.
evidence: This is based on the NMR data comparison between L400S and WT.

claim: The substrate signal observed in LeuT WT samples is not reporting on a combination of S1 and S2 binding.
source: This argues against the possibility that the substrate signal we observe in LeuT WT samples is reporting on a combination of S1 and S2 binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the L400S mutant data.

claim: It would be highly unlikely for an S1 bound substrate and a putative S2 site-bound substrate to have the same chemical shift as the environment of the putative S2 binding site markedly differs from the S1 binding site.
source: Also, we reason that it would be highly unlikely for an S1 bound substrate and a putative S2 site-bound substrate to have the same chemical shift as the environment of the putative S2 binding site markedly differs from the S1 binding site.
evidence: This is based on NMR principles and structural knowledge.

claim: The proposed S2 binding site does not involve direct sodium binding.
source: As a major difference, the proposed S2 binding site does not involve direct sodium binding (Shi et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference Shi et al., 2008.

claim: All LeuT samples used in the present study were prepared in DDM at low concentration to exclude previously reported detrimental effects on the S2 binding site.
source: In conclusion, although all LeuT samples used in the present study were prepared in DDM at low concentration to exclude previously reported detrimental effects on the S2 binding site, we were only able to identify one single substrate signal at 38.2 ppm in the 15N spectra and one set of signals in the 13C spectrum (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used.

claim: Only one single substrate signal at 38.2 ppm was identified in the 15N spectra.
source: In conclusion, although all LeuT samples used in the present study were prepared in DDM at low concentration to exclude previously reported detrimental effects on the S2 binding site, we were only able to identify one single substrate signal at 38.2 ppm in the 15N spectra and one set of signals in the 13C spectrum (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data.

claim: At the current signal-to-noise ratio (~20), species populated less than 5% of the structural ensemble would not be detectable.
source: We note, however, that at our current signal-to-noise ratio (~20), we would not be able to detect species populated less than 5% of the structural ensemble.
evidence: This is based on the signal-to-noise ratio of the NMR data.

claim: Based on the minor change in chemical shift in the F253A (S1) mutant, and the completely unaltered signal for the L400S (S2) mutant, the observable bound leucine is located at the S1 binding site.
source: Based on the minor change in chemical shift in the F253A (S1) mutant, and the completely unaltered signal for the L400S (S2) mutant we reason that the observable bound leucine is located at the S1 binding site, thus supporting the idea that LeuT exhibit one single central binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant NMR data.

claim: LeuT exhibits one single central binding site.
source: Based on the minor change in chemical shift in the F253A (S1) mutant, and the completely unaltered signal for the L400S (S2) mutant we reason that the observable bound leucine is located at the S1 binding site, thus supporting the idea that LeuT exhibit one single central binding site.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the NMR data.

claim: The detection of S2 binding may only be possible upon the complete transition of the transporter towards a specific (yet unknown) conformation.
source: We cannot exclude that the detection of S2 binding may only be possible upon the complete transition of the transporter towards a specific (yet unknown) conformation or that unfavourable crystal contacts might complicate S2 binding.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations of the study.

claim: Unfavourable crystal contacts might complicate S2 binding.
source: We cannot exclude that the detection of S2 binding may only be possible upon the complete transition of the transporter towards a specific (yet unknown) conformation or that unfavourable crystal contacts might complicate S2 binding.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations of the study.

claim: Several crystal structures have shown the binding of antidepressants, which overlaps with the putative S2 site, using these exact conditions.
source: However, several crystal structures have shown the binding of antidepressants, which overlaps with the putative S2 site, using these exact conditions (Singh et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited structural studies.

claim: The S2 substrate binding site, if present, is rather a transient site, responsible for optimal functionality of the transporter.
source: As previously proposed for LeuT (Piscitelli et al., 2010) we speculate that the S2 substrate binding site, if present, is rather a transient site, responsible for optimal functionality of the transporter.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data and cited literature.

claim: LeuT WT was expressed in E. coli C41(DE3) transformed with pET16b encoding C-terminally 8xHis-tagged transporter.
source: LeuT WT was expressed in E. coli C41(DE3) transformed with pET16b encoding C-terminally 8xHis-tagged transporter (expression plasmid was kindly provided by Dr E. Gouaux, Vollum Institute, Portland, Oregon, USA).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Isolated bacterial membranes were solubilized in 1% DDM in the presence of 1 mM 98% 15N-L-Leucine.
source: Briefly, isolated bacterial membranes were solubilized in 1% DDM (Anatrace, USA) in the presence of 1 mM 98% 15N-L-Leucine (Cambridge isotopes, Tewksbury, MA) and the protein was bound to nickel-charged affinity resin (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: LeuT microcrystals are needle-shaped and have a length of 1–10 μm.
source: LeuT microcrystals are needle-shaped and have a length of 1–10 μm.
evidence: This is directly supported by the microscopic image shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rod-shaped microcrystals form within 24 hr.
source: Rod-shaped microcrystals form within 24 hr and can be readily harvested.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the methods.

claim: The pI of L-leucine amine is estimated to be 9.72 ± 0.06.
source: From the sigmoidal curve fit the pI is estimated to be 9.72 ± 0.06.
evidence: This is directly supported by the pH titration data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The signal-to-noise is calculated to be 21.
source: Signal-to-noise is calculated to be 21.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Full width half height (FWHH) of the substrate peak is 31 Hz.
source: Full width half height (FWHH) of the substrate peak is 31 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Despite inequivalent location of the two sodium sites in the LeuT, the coordination mechanism is almost identical which might account for the observation of a single peak in the 23Na-NMR spectrum instead of two distinct peaks.
source: Despite inequivalent location of the two sodium sites in the LeuT, the coordination mechanism is almost identical which might account for the observation of a single peak in the 23Na-NMR spectrum instead of two distinct peaks.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the 23Na-NMR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Minor peak at −8.9 ppm in 23Na-NMR represents the shape of one or two structural sodium molecules.
source: Minor peak at −8.9 ppm represents the shape of one or two structural sodium molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C.

claim: In frozen, lyophilized and proteoliposomes preparations, the signal from the unspecific or unbound leucine completely dominated the spectra.
source: In all other preparations tested (frozen, lyophilized and proteoliposomes) the signal from the unspecific or unbound leucine completely dominated the spectra (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: Free 15N L-Leucine has a distinct chemical shift at 118 ppm.
source: Free 15N L-Leucine has a distinct chemical shift at 118 ppm.
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Microcrystalline samples were produced by large scale sitting drop vapour diffusion method.
source: Microcrystalline samples were produced by large scale sitting drop vapour diffusion method.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: The crystallization was carried out at 18°C.
source: The crystallization was carried out at 18°C.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used.

claim: After approximately 20 hr a white precipitate could be harvested by centrifugation.
source: After approximately 20 hr a white precipitate could be harvested by centrifugation and transferred directly to the rotor.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.
